title: Thomas (3 July)
hook: the doubter who, tradition says, took the gospel to India

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first martyrs of Rome, a crowd with no names, known to us through Tacitus. Your line was no names, all known.

"Doubting Thomas." People say it at work about the colleague who wants to see the numbers, and at home about the kid who won't believe the stove is hot. It has stuck to him. But in John's Gospel, the first time we hear this man speak, he offers to die. And when he finally believes, what he says about Jesus is startlingly plain. Today, a witness with a nickname he might not have chosen. Thomas.
screen: `DOUBTING THOMAS.` → `THE MAN WHO OFFERED TO DIE.` → `STARTLINGLY PLAIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First scene. Jesus decides to go back toward Judea, where people had tried to stone him, because his friend Lazarus has died. The disciples protest. Thomas, John says, "who is called Didymus," Greek for twin, turns to the others: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Grim, maybe. But brave. Second scene. On the evening of the resurrection day, Jesus appears to the disciples, and Thomas isn't there. They tell him. He refuses to take it secondhand. "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." That's the line that earned the nickname. Third scene, eight days later. Thomas is with them. Jesus comes, stands among them, and offers Thomas exactly what he asked for: put your finger here, see my hands. John never says Thomas touches him. What he says is: "Thomas answered, and said to him: My Lord and my God." Not teacher. Not prophet. Catholics hear in it a full confession of faith in Jesus, from the man who wouldn't believe secondhand. Jesus answers: blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed. Then the Gospel goes quiet about him. Tradition carries on. It says Thomas went east, preached in India, and died there as a martyr. Some Christians in India, above all the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, trace their church to him. Historians debate the details. For those churches, the tradition is their own story.
screen: `LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE.` · `UNLESS I SEE, I WILL NOT BELIEVE.` · `HE NEVER SAYS HE TOUCHED.` · `TRADITION: EAST TO INDIA.` · then, large: `MY LORD AND MY GOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the churches of India, old communities and new, in cities and villages, some small and under pressure, and picture a family going to church on a hot morning, in a language you may not know. If you pray, say Thomas's words slowly, once, my Lord and my God, and offer them for those communities. If you don't, simply wish them peace and safety.
Thomas. The apostle called the Twin, who doubted, then said my Lord and my God, and who, tradition says, carried the gospel to India.
Your line: my lord and my god. The plainest words came from the one who asked to see. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Church keeps the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle on 3 July; in India, the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala keep it as the feast of the apostle they trace their church to.

chat.says: Isn't Thomas just the apostle who didn't believe?
options: He doubted, but he also offered to die with Jesus, and said: my Lord and my God.
Yes. He never believed, and left the other apostles before Jesus appeared again.
He doubted the whole time, and only came to believe after he reached India.
chat.meaning: John shows Thomas ready to die with Jesus, then refusing to believe secondhand, then making the plainest confession of all: my Lord and my God.
